item.title: International Collegiate Programming Contest
item.description:
Introduction

The International Collegiate Programming Contest (ICPC) is a team programming competition. This guide helps UWF students prepare for Division 2 (D2) of the Southeast USA Regional. Start with problems you can solve using a scan, a frequency count, sorting, or a small search. Practice turning a correct idea into an accepted submission on a shared workstation.

Levels of competition

Students can start with local practice contests. The ICPC competition progresses through regionals and regional championships to the World Finals. This guide focuses on the Southeast Regional.

item.title: Problem A - Snakey String With Solution
item.description:
A snakey string is a fancy rendering of an otherwise normal string of text. When a string is made snakey, it is placed on a 2D grid such that the following conditions are met:

  • The first character of the string is on the first column of the grid, the second on the second column, …, and the last on the last column.
  • Each character in the string occupies either the row directly above or directly below the row of the previous character.

item.title: How to Use the ICPC Division 2 TRD
item.description:
Keep the Team Reference Document (TRD) open beside this guide. Find the topic in the PDF, work through the example here, then adapt the PDF’s listing to a small problem. During timed practice, try finding the same listing from the PDF index alone. Download the 25-page TRD · ICPC Division 2 preparation guide

Page 1 · Read the index and notation

The page numbers below match the PDF’s printed numbers. A listing often shows just the function or loop you need. Put it into the page 3 starter, declare and read the inputs it expects, and decide what to print. For example, a function that returns an index may need you to print that index plus one if the problem numbers positions from one.

item.title: Problem B - Blind Bottles
item.description: You are playing the Blind Bottles game. There are n bottles, each with a unique color. The game host arranges them into one row, keeping their ordering a secret. Your goal is to determine the host’s ordering by making guesses. In each guess, you provide one ordering of the bottles. The host will tell you the number of bottles in your ordering that are in the correct positions. You win the game when you make a guess that places all the bottles in their correct positions.

item.title: Problem B - Blind Bottles — Solution
item.description:
1. The Game in One Minute

  • There are n bottles, each labeled 1..n, arranged in a secret order.
  • A guess is a line of n numbers (a rearrangement of 1..n).
  • After each guess, you’re told how many positions are exactly right.
  • You win when all positions are right.

Our goal: figure out the secret order using at most 10,000 guesses for n ≤ 100.

item.title: Problem C - One Way Only
item.description: You’ve been tasked with mapping out one of the most dangerous hiking routes deep within the Amazon rainforest. This hiking route exists on a rectangular area of land that has been tiled into a 2D grid with $r$ rows and $c$ columns. Hikers who dare attempt this trail begin on the top-left tile $(1,1)$ and work their way down to tile $(r,c)$. In order to finish as fast as possible, every hiker will move only rightward or downward during their hike.

item.title: Problem J - Game of Nines
item.description:
You are playing a simple game of adding digits. You are given a list of single digits between 0 and 8 (inclusive).

In each move, you may choose any two digits a and b, add a to b, and replace b with the sum a + b. If a + b ≥ 10, keep only the units digit (e.g., 5 + 8 becomes 3; 4 + 6 becomes 0).

Whenever the sum is 9, the result is eliminated immediately and cannot participate in further additions. Note that you cannot add a digit to itself, but you may choose two digits a and b that have the same value.

item.title: Problem J - Game of Nines — Solution
item.description:
1. Story-style intuition

Picture your digits $0$–$8$ as tokens on a 10-hour clock (positions $0$ through $9$). When you “add digit $a$ to digit $b$”, you move token $b$ forward by $a$ ticks around the clock. If you land exactly on $9$, that token disappears.

Two important facts drive everything:

  1. Helpers don’t get used up.

    A digit you use as an adder stays on the table. You can reuse it indefinitely.

  2. Only the total step size matters.

    Adders are reusable and order doesn’t matter, so what matters is the set of step sizes you can produce in total modulo $10$.
